newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet approves lower 1997 customs duties.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet approves lower 1997 customs duties.

text.p: The Polish government on Tuesday approved customs tariffs for 1997 which envisage lowering the average duty on imports to 5.8 percent from this year's 7.5 percent, the acting foreign trade minister said.
"The tariff takes into account all our obligations stemming from international treaties," Janusz Kaczurba told a news briefing.

Poland belongs to the World Trade Organisation (WTO). Its treaties with the European Union and the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) states envisage phasing out all customs duties by the year 2002 in trade with these countries. @
Sensitive sectors such as steel, textiles, fuels and cars will enjoy the longest protection period.
Kaczurba said that under the 1997 tariffs, the average duty for agricultural products would go down to 14.1 percent from the current 15.8 percent.
Duty for petrol from European Union countries will be reduced to 13 percent from 15 percent now and that for diesel will go down to 20 percent from 25 percent. @

Under the association agreement with the EU, the petrol duty should have been reduced even further next year. But after lengthy negotiations Brussels has suggested it might agree to Poland extending the protection period for its oil industry.

According to the Rzeczpospolita financial daily, Poland will also maintain this year's nine percent duty for steel products in 1997, even though it was originally supposed to fall to six percent under its accord with the EU.

Rzeczpospolita said a plan to restructure the steel industry, tentatively approved by the EU, provides for abolishing the steel duty in 2001 and not in 2000 as agreed earlier. The pace of phasing out the duty would also be slower. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
